🎯 CENTRAL QUESTION
When the structures of civilization fall away, what is left of us: the better part or the worse?
📚 THIS WEEK'S LESSONS
Writing StyleImagery: The Five Senses as an Author's Choice
LiteratureThe Platform and the Conch (read Ch. 1)
Writing StyleDiction and Connotation
LiteratureRalph's First Speech: How Ritual and the Conch Create Order (read Ch. 2; copy by hand)
Check-upDiscussion: Is Ralph a Leader?
⭐ OPTIONAL · A SHORT BONUS READING
Poetry Pairing: “The Second Coming,” W.B. Yeats
Optional and ungraded; not one of the five lessons. Yeats's 1920 poem about a world where order breaks down (“the centre cannot hold”) pairs with the collapse of order on Golding's island. 10 to 15 minutes.
📤 WORK FOR THE WEEK
1
Week 1 Daily Practice · handwritten notebook, photo upload
Copywork of Ralph's first speech, a retell of the platform scene, and imagery and diction practice.
2
Week 1 Quick Write · typed Word document
Annotate the conch and platform scenes in your own copy. What is Golding showing about order?
3
Discussion · forum post + one reply
Is Ralph a leader? Defend your answer from the text, and answer one objection to your view.
🏆 MODULE CAPSTONE
This module ends in Week 7 with a Final Argumentative Essay on the central question above. Evidence is gathered from the first chapter onward.
Three passages from the novel are memorized by the end of the module: the conch passage, Simon's death, and the closing lines. The first begins this week.
📝 ONGOING THIS MODULE
●
Memory work. Begin learning Passage 1, the conch passage, where Ralph first calls the boys together. Learn a few lines each day.
📚 ONE IMPORTANT NOTE ABOUT THE BOOK
Lord of the Flies is still under copyright, so its text is not reproduced in this course. Read from your own copy of the novel. When a lesson asks you to copy or quote a line, copy it from your own book.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write an original short story that unsettles the reader through Jackson’s technique (compression, buried hints, refusal to explain) rather than gore, set in an ordinary world that hides one quiet tradition. The submission is the Week 2 draft, revised with a partner’s feedback. The story explores the module question without spelling it out: what kinds of evil hide inside a tradition that no one any longer remembers the reason for?
🎯 TASK
Write an original 1-to-2-page story that imitates Jackson’s technique: compression, buried foreshadowing, and the refusal to explain.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Write a story of 1 to 2 pages (about 400 to 700 words) set in an ordinary, believable world that hides one unsettling tradition.
2
Compress. Begin in the middle of the action, cut the warm-up, and imply more than is explained.
3
Bury the foreshadowing. Plant at least one quiet hint that a first-time reader could miss, and that pays off at the turn.
4
Refuse to explain. Leave at least one thing deliberately blank (the origin, the reason, the meaning). The story must be original; do not retell "The Lottery" or borrow Jackson’s characters or sentences.
📊 HOW THIS IS GRADED
Criterion Excellent Proficient Developing Beginning
Imitation of Jackson’s technique (compression, buried foreshadowing, refusal to explain) All three tools are used with control: the story is tight, the hint is genuinely buried, and a key thing is left blank on purpose. All three tools are present and mostly effective, with only minor slips. One or two tools appear, but the hint is too obvious, the story over-explains, or it runs long. Little evidence of the three tools; the story explains everything or hides nothing.
Narrative craft (an ordinary world made unsettling; a turn that lands) A believable, ordinary world is built quickly and turned unsettling; the turn surprises yet feels earned. A clear ordinary world and a turn that mostly lands. The world or the turn is present but thin; the surprise feels unearned or flat. Little sense of an ordinary world or a meaningful turn.
Control of dread and foreshadowing Unease builds steadily and quietly; the buried hint pays off and the calm surface makes it land harder. A sense of dread develops and the hint connects to the ending. Some unease, but it is too loud, too early, or disconnected from the ending. Little control of dread; tension is absent or telegraphed.
Clarity and correctness of prose Clean, controlled sentences; varied structure; errors are rare and do not distract. Mostly clean sentences; minor errors that do not obscure meaning. Several run-ons, fragments, or splices that slow the reader. Frequent errors that often make meaning unclear.

2Dramatic ReadingABOUT 3 MINUTES
›Choose a passage of roughly 150 to 300 words where a character is under pressure: deciding, arguing, afraid, or hiding something.
›Read it aloud as that character. Decide before you record what they want in this moment, then let your pace, volume and pauses show it.
›Then talk for about a minute: who is this character, what do they want here, and what did you do with your voice to show it? Name one specific choice you made.
3Make the CaseABOUT 3 MINUTES
You are a guest on a books podcast and the host has given you three minutes to make one argument. House rule of the show: you have to take the side most listeners will not.
›Name what you are arguing about, and say where it falls in the book. Pick something people genuinely disagree over: a moral dilemma, a turn nobody saw coming, or a decision a character made that readers still argue about.
›Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
›Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
›Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
›Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
4A Different EndingABOUT 3 MINUTES
Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.
›Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate. The rest of this only works if your listener knows what you are changing.
›Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?
›Explain why yours is better for this book. Not happier, and not kinder to your favourite character, but truer to what the story has been about. Name the idea or theme you are serving.
›Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
A letter to the editor argues one position in half a page to a general reader. This letter answers the question below in one page, in the writer’s own voice.
✎ WRITE AS YOURSELF
Write in own voice, to a newspaper of the present. Do not write as a citizen of Maycomb in 1935, and do not invent a character. The novel supplies the evidence and the occasion.
🎯 THE QUESTION
Is it worth doing the right thing when you already know it will not change the outcome?
Take a side: it is worth it, it is not, or it depends on something that can be named precisely. Any of the three can earn full credit. Refusing to decide cannot.
📝 THE FORM: HOW A LETTER TO THE EDITOR IS BUILT
This is business correspondence, so it follows a business structure. Use all six parts, in this order.
1. The writer’s address and the date, at the top, on the left.
2. The recipient, on the next lines: the editor's title and the paper's name and address.
3. A salutation: Dear Editor, or To the Editor:
4. The body, in three short paragraphs. Open by naming the position in the first two sentences. Support it in the middle, including one specific moment from the novel, cited by chapter. Close by saying what the reader should do or think differently about.
5. A closing: Sincerely, or Respectfully,
6. The writer’s name, and your town.
✅ WHAT THIS FORM REQUIRES
One issue only.
A formal register, and a civil one. The reader is a stranger who may disagree.
One page, no longer. Roughly 250 to 350 words in the body.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
An original scene in Scout’s voice: invent a new moment in Maycomb that the novel does not show, set during the year the novel covers, and narrate it as Scout: plain, observant, lightly humorous, and quietly aware that the grown-up world holds more than she can yet name. The scene is one of three converging projects; the Final Essay draws on what writing in Lee’s voice showed about the central question.
🎯 TASK
Write an original 1-to-2-page scene set in Maycomb, narrated by Scout in Lee’s voice, that captures her tone, her eye for detail, and the gap between what she sees and what she understands.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Write a scene of 1 to 2 pages (about 400 to 700 words). Invent a small new moment in Maycomb: a porch conversation, an errand into town, a walk past a familiar house. Do not retell a scene the novel already gives.
2
Use Scout’s voice. Narrate in the first person, in a plain, direct, lightly funny tone. Scout reports what she sees clearly while showing that she does not yet grasp everything the moment means.
3

🎯 THE CENTRAL QUESTION
What does justice cost in a community that does not yet want it, and what does it ask of the few who serve it?
Answer through the novel. Possible positions: the cost falls hardest on those with the least power, the few who serve justice pay in ways the town never repays, or the trial changes Maycomb in ways the verdict alone does not show. Any clear position can earn full marks if it is defended well.

›Take the unpopular side and say it in your first sentence. If most readers think the character was right, argue that they were wrong. If nobody could disagree with your claim, it is not an argument yet.
›Give two pieces of evidence from the text: a line, a scene, something a character says or does. Say roughly where each one falls.
›Answer the strongest objection, the one the host would come back at you with. State it fairly first, then answer it.
›Land it. Finish with one sentence a listener would still be turning over after the episode ends.
4A Different EndingABOUT 3 MINUTES
Only take this one if you finished the book. You are going to replace the ending, and you cannot rewrite an ending you never got to.
›Say how the book actually ends, in two or three sentences. Be accurate. The rest of this only works if your listener knows what you are changing.
›Name the exact point where your version branches off, then describe your ending in detail. What happens, who it happens to, and how does it finish?
›Explain why yours is better for this book. Not happier, and not kinder to your favourite character, but truer to what the story has been about. Name the idea or theme you are serving.
›Say what your ending costs. Every ending gives something up. Name what is lost by not keeping the one the author wrote.
Full credit
 
☐Clear evidence the book was read.
☐Points at a specific moment or line, not the story in general.
☐Says something original: a judgement, a disagreement, a question.
☐Audible the whole way through.

TRACKAudio only is complete. Video is permitted, never required.

When Truth Is Not Enough
Discussion · 10 pts
💬 THIS WEEK’S QUESTION
This week the testimony made the truth plain: the accusing story fell apart, and Tom Robinson’s account held. Yet the town has already decided. The chapters force a hard question about justice in a community that does not yet want it.
📝 YOUR POST (5 TO 8 SENTENCES)
Answer: Whose testimony carries the most weight, and why does it not change the outcome? Cite one specific moment of testimony from Chapters 18 to 20 and explain what it makes plain. Then connect it to the central question: what does this scene show about what justice costs in a community that does not yet want it? Then name the strongest objection to the reading and answer it. Some readers argue the trial does matter, even without changing the verdict, because of what it reveals or sets in motion.
End your post with one sentence beginning: "The strongest objection to my reading is… but I still think…"
💬 YOUR REPLY (2 TO 4 SENTENCES)
Reply to a classmate who chose a different testimony or reached a different conclusion. Say what is strong in their reading, then add what else the testimony shows, courteously.
📋 HOW THIS DISCUSSION RUNS
1. Deadlines. Post by midweek. Reply by the end of the week. A late post leaves no time for replies.
2. Length limits. Stay inside the sentence counts given above, for the post and for the reply. A long post takes the floor from later posters.
3. Open with the vote. Begin the post with one word on its own line: YES or NO, answering this question about how Lee built these chapters. Does Lee write the trial so that its outcome ever seems genuinely in doubt? The teacher posts the class tally at the end of the week. The vote concerns the author's design, not whether the verdict was just: the novel is not ambiguous about that. The vote shows where the room stands before anyone has argued.
4. Take notes as the thread grows. Write down the two strongest points not thought of independently, each with the name of the classmate who made it. Crediting the person who changed one’s mind is part of arguing honestly.
✅ HOW THIS IS SCORED
Full credit: a clear claim about which testimony weighs most, one specific moment cited from the novel, a link to the central question, a fairly stated objection with your answer, and a substantive reply to a classmate.
